passage: Teacher's note, Class 10 assembly, Monday. Tejas (15) gave his first assembly talk today, on why our school should start a seed library. Last week in rehearsal he spoke to the floor and rushed through in two minutes. We worked on a shape: open with a short story, three points, close with one request. Today his knees were visibly shaking at the mic. He opened with the story of his grandmother's tomato seeds, and a few juniors laughed at the right moment. Halfway through he lost his place. He stopped, breathed, glanced at his card, looked at the front row and carried on. He ended by asking, 'Who'll bring one packet of seeds?' Hands went up. Next step: I've asked him to coach the Class 8 speakers. — Hrithik Sir

qa.q: What was Tejas's talk about?
qa.a: Why the school should start a seed library.

qa.q: How can you tell Tejas was afraid at the mic?
qa.a: His knees were visibly shaking, and in rehearsal he had spoken to the floor and rushed.

qa.q: What helped Tejas recover when he lost his place?
qa.a: He paused, breathed, checked his card and looked at the front row before continuing, instead of panicking.

qa.q: How might the juniors in the audience have experienced the talk?
qa.a: They were drawn in by the grandmother's seed story and felt invited to act when Tejas asked for seeds.

grounding: A teacher records a teen structuring a talk, handling stage fear and holding an audience.

passage: Thursday, 10 pm. Youth parliament done!!! Writing this before I forget how it felt. Woke up at five with my stomach in knots. Hansa made me practise twice on the terrace, once to her and once to the water tank, and made me slow down. She said, 'Say your first line like you're telling me a secret.' At the district hall there were about two hundred people. My voice cracked on 'Honourable Speaker' and someone giggled. I wanted to vanish. But I did the thing: feet flat, one breath, looked at the kind uncle in the second row. Then I told the story of our village's broken handpump, and the hall went quiet. Quiet in a good way. I actually held them. Me! Santosh!

qa.q: Where did Santosh practise before the youth parliament?
qa.a: On the terrace, once to Hansa and once to the water tank.

qa.q: What did Santosh feel when his voice cracked and someone giggled?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and wanted to vanish, but then steadied himself.

qa.q: Which of Santosh's techniques could help another nervous speaker?
qa.a: Planting feet flat, taking one breath, finding a kind face and opening with a real story.

qa.q: How might Hansa feel reading this diary entry?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and happy that her practice sessions helped him hold the hall. 😊

grounding: A teen records managing stage fear and holding an audience with a practised talk.

passage: Last year I didn't think I had a problem. I'd open the video app 'for five minutes' after dinner and look up and it'd be midnight. I thought I just had weak willpower. Then my friend Thomas, who's into coding, showed me something. He said, 'It's built that way. Autoplay, the endless scroll, the little red dots. They test which colour makes you tap more.' I laughed, but it stung. It felt like being played. So I tried an experiment. I turned off autoplay and all notifications for a week. The first two days I kept reaching for the phone, weirdly itchy. By Friday I read half a novel. I still watch videos. I just choose them now, mostly.

qa.q: What features did Thomas point out in the video app?
qa.a: Autoplay, the endless scroll and the little red dots.

qa.q: Why did Thomas's explanation 'sting' for the narrator?
qa.a: The narrator realised the app was designed to keep them hooked, which felt like being played rather than simply having weak willpower.

qa.q: What was sensible about the narrator's experiment?
qa.a: The narrator changed the design traps they could control, autoplay and notifications, and watched what happened for a week.

qa.q: How might Thomas see the narrator's change?
qa.a: He might be glad his coding knowledge helped a friend take back some control of their time.

grounding: A teen reflects on learning how app features are designed to hold attention and adjusting their own use.

passage: Counsellor's note, Digital Life elective, Class 9. For the attention-trap project, Afreen (14) logged every notification on her phone for three days. She came to me looking shaken: 'Ma'am, 212 in one day. Most were from one game app telling me my streak would die.' She had never noticed the streak made her open the game even when she was bored with it. In her presentation, she showed the class a slide of her tally and asked, 'Who decided I had to keep a streak?' Several students laughed nervously. I saw two quietly open their settings. Next step: I'll invite Afreen to help design a class challenge on switching off non-essential alerts, and ask the class to reflect afterwards rather than preach. — Mrs Jagdish

qa.q: How many notifications did Afreen log in one day?
qa.a: 212 in one day.

qa.q: Why did Afreen look shaken when she came to the counsellor?
qa.a: She realised how many alerts were steering her, especially the streak pushing her to play a game she was bored with.

qa.q: Why is Mrs Jagdish's plan to have the class reflect rather than preach a good one?
qa.a: Students are more likely to change their habits when they discover the traps themselves, as Afreen did.

qa.q: What might the two students who opened their settings have been thinking?
qa.a: They were probably recognising the same patterns in their own phones and wanting to switch some alerts off.

grounding: A counsellor records a teen discovering how notifications and streaks are designed to keep users engaged.

passage:
Dear Tanvir,
Maasi said you just started posting, so big-sister-cousin advice, whether you want it or not.
Last month I applied for the student editor post at college. In the interview, the teacher said, 'We had a look at your public profile.' My stomach dropped. At thirteen, I'd left a nasty comment under a classmate's dance video. I'd forgotten it. They hadn't. I explained, apologised, said I'd changed. I still got the post, but I felt about six inches tall.
So, three things. Before you post, ask: would I be fine with a teacher, a future boss or Nani seeing this? Screenshots last forever, even after you delete. And be the kind of person online you are at dinner.
Love,
Sudha didi

qa.q: What had Sudha done at thirteen that came up in her interview?
qa.a: She had left a nasty comment under a classmate's dance video.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel when the teacher mentioned her public profile?
qa.a: Her stomach dropped and she felt ashamed, about six inches tall, even though she had changed.

qa.q: Which of Sudha's tips would help Tanvir most before posting?
qa.a: Asking whether Tanvir would be fine with a teacher, future boss or Nani seeing it, since posts and screenshots can last.

qa.q: How might the classmate from the dance video feel if they knew about that comment years later?
qa.a: They might still remember the hurt, showing that online comments can affect people long after they're written.

grounding: A teen writes to her cousin about how old posts and comments persist and shape reputation.

passage: Okay Nirmala, you asked why I'm so careful now. So, last year, at Diwali, I snapped a photo of Harpreet mid-sneeze with laddoo crumbs everywhere. Honestly hilarious. I posted it with a caption and it got loads of likes. Harpreet asked me to delete it that night and I did, straight away. I thought that was the end. Two months later, it turned up as a sticker in the class group. Someone had screenshotted it. People sent it every time he spoke. He stopped talking in the group. And the worst part? Everyone knew I'd started it. I apologised properly, face to face. Now I've got a rule: if it's someone else's face, I ask. If it's mine, I think twice.

qa.q: What happened to the photo two months after the narrator deleted it?
qa.a: It turned up as a sticker in the class group because someone had screenshotted it.

qa.q: How did Harpreet seem to feel when the sticker kept being sent?
qa.a: He seemed hurt and embarrassed, since he stopped talking in the group.

qa.q: Why is the narrator's new rule a sensible one?
qa.a: It respects other people's say over their own image and makes the narrator pause before posting anything, even about themselves.

qa.q: How might Harpreet see the narrator after the face-to-face apology?
qa.a: He might forgive them slowly, though the lasting sticker could still sting.

grounding: A teen recounts how a deleted post persisted through screenshots and harmed a friend's reputation.

subtype: Using AI Tools Ethically & Verifying Outputs
passage:
Subject: About my history essay
Dear Yamini Ma'am,
I want to be honest before you grade my essay on the Salt March. I used a chatbot to help me start. It gave me a neat paragraph and three sources. When I looked for the sources in the library catalogue, one book didn't exist at all, and one quote had the wrong year. I felt a bit sick, because I had almost submitted it.
So I started over. I used the chatbot only to ask questions like 'What caused this?' and then checked everything in our textbook and two real books. The essay is in my words now, and it's shorter. If the first draft counts against me, I understand.
Regards,
Ramesh, 11-B

qa.q: What was wrong with the sources the chatbot gave Ramesh?
qa.a: One book didn't exist, and one quote had the wrong year.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh feel 'a bit sick' on checking the sources?
qa.a: Ramesh realised the essay had nearly gone in with invented facts that had never been checked.

qa.q: What is sensible about how Ramesh used the chatbot the second time?
qa.a: Ramesh used it only to raise questions and then checked every answer in real books, writing the essay in their own words.

qa.q: How might Yamini Ma'am see Ramesh's email?
qa.a: She would probably value Ramesh's honesty and see that Ramesh learned to verify, even if the essay is shorter.

grounding: A teen writes about checking an AI tool's citations and using it without outsourcing their thinking.

passage: You asked on the school radio how I use AI for studying, so here's the honest version. I'm Tanvir, Class 11. When I got stuck on limits in calculus, I asked a chatbot to explain it like I'm twelve. That actually helped. But then I'd close it and do the textbook problems myself, on paper. My friend Damini did it differently. She had it solve her whole assignment. Full marks. Then in the unit test she stared at question one for twenty minutes, completely blank. She told me later she felt like a fraud. Also, once it gave me a wrong answer with total confidence, so I always check with the book or with Sir. It's a tutor, not a replacement brain.

qa.q: What topic in calculus was Tanvir stuck on?
qa.a: Limits.

qa.q: How did Damini feel after the unit test?
qa.a: She felt like a fraud, because she couldn't do the work herself after the tool had done her assignment.

qa.q: What is the difference between Tanvir's and Damini's approach?
qa.a: Tanvir used the tool to understand and then practised alone, while Damini let it do the work, so she learned nothing.

qa.q: How might Sir react if he learned how Damini got full marks?
qa.a: He would likely be disappointed and want her to redo the work so she actually learns.

grounding: A teen explains using AI to learn while checking its claims, contrasted with outsourcing thinking.

passage: For two weeks, someone called 'Rhea' had been messaging Arnab, fifteen, on a gaming chat: compliments, music, jokes about their Kolkata school. Then, one night in his room in their Salt Lake flat, the tone changed. 'Send 5,000 by tomorrow or I'll send our chats, edited, to your whole class.' Arnab's hands went cold. He hadn't done anything wrong, but edited chats could look like anything. He almost opened his savings app. Instead, heart pounding, he knocked on his sister Kalyani's door. She read it once. 'Don't pay. Don't reply. Screenshot everything.' They woke their parents together. That night Baba helped Arnab report the account on the platform and on the government cybercrime portal. Arnab barely slept, but for the first time in hours, he could breathe.

qa.q: What did 'Rhea' threaten to do if Arnab didn't pay?
qa.a: Send edited versions of their chats to his whole class.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when the threat arrived?
qa.a: He was frightened and panicked, with cold hands, worried that edited chats could make him look bad.

qa.q: Why were Kalyani's instructions the right ones?
qa.a: Not paying or replying stops giving the blackmailer power, and screenshots keep evidence for reporting.

qa.q: How might it feel for Arnab's parents to be woken with this news?
qa.a: They would likely be shaken but relieved he came to them before paying anything.

grounding: Shows a teen recognising blackmail through online contact and reporting it to trusted adults.

passage: 'Kashish di, look, a modelling scout messaged me!' Avni held out her phone across the kitchen table. 'He says I have the face for ads.' Kashish read it. 'He wants more photos, “casual ones”, and wants you to keep it secret from your parents till the contract?' 'He said it's normal. Surprise for them.' 'Hmm. Does a real agency ask a fourteen-year-old to hide things from her parents?' Avni hesitated. 'I guess not.' 'And why's he in a hurry? “Reply tonight or the chance is gone.”' 'That's weird too.' 'Secret, hurry, photos. Three red flags.' Avni went quiet. 'I already sent one selfie.' 'That's okay. It's not your fault, and you did right to tell me. Let's block, report, and tell Mami together, right now.' Avni nodded, a little shaky.

qa.q: What did the 'scout' ask Avni to keep secret?
qa.a: He asked her to keep it secret from her parents until the contract.

qa.q: Why did Avni go quiet after Kashish named the three red flags?
qa.a: She was realising the message was not a real opportunity and worried because she had already sent one selfie.

qa.q: How did Kashish respond helpfully when Avni admitted sending a selfie?
qa.a: She stayed calm, told Avni it was not her fault, and turned straight to blocking, reporting and telling Mami together that same day.

qa.q: What would change if Avni had kept the chat secret as asked?
qa.a: She would have faced the pressure alone, making it easier for him to push for more photos.

grounding: Shows a teen recognising grooming tactics online and reporting with a trusted adult.

passage: Week one: Anjali, sixteen, yawned through the first period every day. She'd been watching short videos in bed until two. 'Just one more,' she'd tell herself, forty times. Her brother Joseph teased, 'Panda eyes!' She didn't laugh. Week two, Sunday: She checked her screen-time page and felt sick. Five hours after eleven p.m. across the week. She wrote on a sticky note: 'Phone charges in the hall at 11. Alarm clock, not phone.' Joseph raised an eyebrow. 'You'll last one night.' Week four: She had slipped twice, once for a cricket final, and started again the next day both times. First period felt different now. 'No panda eyes,' Joseph admitted, and she threw a pillow at him.

qa.q: What rule did Anjali write on her sticky note?
qa.a: The phone charges in the hall at 11, and she uses an alarm clock, not her phone.

qa.q: What did Anjali feel when she checked her screen-time page?
qa.a: She felt sick, shocked by how many late-night hours she was losing.

qa.q: What went right after Anjali slipped?
qa.a: She restarted the limit the very next day instead of giving up entirely.

qa.q: How might Joseph's view of his sister's plan change over the weeks?
qa.a: He went from doubting she'd last a night to admitting the change was working.

grounding: Over several weeks a teen notices compulsive late-night scrolling and sets a personal limit.

passage: Kamal, you think your Nani doesn't understand games? Let me tell you about your Suresh mama. When he was fifteen, a video game parlour opened near our market. Ten coins a game. He began going after school, then instead of tuition. He'd come home at night saying he'd been at a friend's. His eyes were red, he slept in class. One day his teacher came to our house. I wasn't angry first; I was frightened. He cried and said, 'Amma, I can't stop, I keep thinking about the next level.' We made a plan together: the parlour only on Sundays, and I'd walk him to tuition. He hated it for a month. Then he got better at studies, and cricket. You see the tiredness in your own eyes, beta?

qa.q: What did Suresh start skipping to go to the parlour?
qa.a: He began going to the parlour instead of tuition.

qa.q: What did Suresh feel when he told his mother he couldn't stop?
qa.a: He felt out of control and upset, crying because he kept thinking about the next level.

qa.q: What worked in the plan Suresh and his mother made?
qa.a: It set a clear limit together, only Sundays, and added support by walking him to tuition.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel hearing that Suresh mama struggled in the same way?
qa.a: Kamal might feel less judged and more willing to look honestly at their own tiredness and gaming.

grounding: A grandmother recalls a teen noticing compulsive gaming and setting limits with family help.

passage: Irfan, you've been skipping dinner and doing push-ups at midnight, I've seen. Sit, let me tell you something. At sixteen I had a poster of an action hero on my wall, all muscles. I looked at my thin arms in the mirror every morning and felt like a joke. So I started skipping meals and running in the heat, thinking I'd get that shape faster. At football practice one day, everything went white and I sat down hard on the ground. Coach Dsouza called my father, and we went to the doctor. The doctor said my body was still growing and needed fuel. Coach told me, 'That poster has lights and makeup and a team behind it.' I started eating properly and training slowly. Talk to me before you copy some poster, hah?

qa.q: What happened to the narrator at football practice?
qa.a: Everything went white and the narrator sat down hard on the ground.

qa.q: How did the narrator feel as a teen looking in the mirror?
qa.a: Like a joke, comparing their thin arms with the muscular hero on the poster.

qa.q: Why does the narrator ask Irfan to talk to them?
qa.a: The narrator has seen Irfan skipping dinner and training at midnight, and wants Irfan to get support before harming their health.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel hearing that the narrator went through the same thing?
qa.a: Irfan might feel less alone and more open to changing those habits without feeling judged. 🤍

grounding: An elder recalls teenage body comparison and harmful habits, and a healthier path with trusted adults.

passage: Swimming class started in twenty minutes, and the changing room was loud, steamy and crowded. Darshan, fifteen, stood in the corner with his T-shirt still on. He'd grown softer around the middle this year, and the boys in the reels he scrolled all looked carved from stone. He thought about pretending to have a cold. Madhav, already in his trunks, flicked water at him. 'You coming or what?' 'Maybe I'll sit this one out.' Madhav looked at him properly. 'Dude, half those guys online have filters. You beat me in freestyle last month.' Darshan remembered that race, the burn in his arms, the fun of it. He pulled off the T-shirt quickly before he could change his mind. In the water, he forgot about it.

qa.q: How long was it until swimming class started?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Darshan think about pretending to have a cold?
qa.a: He felt self-conscious about his body compared with the boys in the reels and wanted to avoid being seen.

qa.q: What helped Darshan choose to swim?
qa.a: Madhav reminded him that online images are filtered and that his body could win races, so he focused on what it can do.

qa.q: What might Madhav have noticed that made him look at Darshan properly?
qa.a: He probably noticed Darshan hesitating in his T-shirt and sensed something was wrong beyond laziness.

grounding: Shows a teen handling body comparison with idealised images and choosing a healthy activity.

passage: Monday: Sudha, fourteen, came home and her little sister Damini asked to borrow her pencil box. 'Why do you always TAKE my things?' Sudha shouted, and slammed the door. Later she felt awful and didn't know why she had exploded. Thursday: Sudha started a note on her phone: 'Moods.' She wrote down when she'd snapped. Hungry after school. Tired. Too many tests. She noticed it came in waves, often from nowhere. Mummy said her body was changing a lot and it was common, but she could still choose what to do. The next Tuesday: Damini peeked in. Sudha felt the heat rise. 'Dami, I'm in a mood. Give me ten minutes. Not about you.' After a snack, she called Damini back to play ludo.

qa.q: What did Damini ask to borrow on Monday?
qa.a: Sudha's pencil box.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel after slamming the door on Monday?
qa.a: She felt awful and confused about why she had exploded over something small.

qa.q: What did Sudha do on Tuesday that could help other teens with sudden moods?
qa.a: She named her mood, asked for a short break and explained it wasn't the other person's fault.

qa.q: How might Damini experience the difference between Monday and Tuesday?
qa.a: On Monday she felt shouted at for nothing, but on Tuesday she knew it wasn't about her and got to play later. 🙂

grounding: Shows a teen noticing sudden irritable moods and choosing how to act despite them.

passage: Jeevan, you slammed your door three times this week. No, I'm not scolding. I'll tell you about me at fourteen. One minute I'd be laughing with my friends, and the next I'd want to throw my books out of the window. I once shouted at my father because the dal was too salty, then cried in the bathroom, not knowing why. My mother said, 'Rashmi, your body is changing, the storms will come. You can't stop the rain, but you can hold the umbrella.' She taught me to go for a walk around the building before saying anything. It didn't always work. But more often, by the end of the walk, the storm had passed. Want to walk with me now?

qa.q: What did young Rashmi shout at her father about?
qa.a: That the dal was too salty.

qa.q: How did young Rashmi feel after shouting at her father?
qa.a: She felt confused and upset, crying in the bathroom without knowing why.

qa.q: What does Rashmi suggest Jeevan try when a mood hits?
qa.a: Walking around the building before saying anything, to let the storm pass.

qa.q: What might Jeevan feel when Rashmi says this is not a scolding?
qa.a: Jeevan might feel relieved and understood, and more willing to talk about those moods.

grounding: An elder recalls teenage mood shifts and a strategy for choosing how to act despite them.

passage: The science camp was in the district town, an hour away by bus, and it ended at six in the evening. Zainab, sixteen, knew Abbu would say no. He was nervous about her travelling back after dark. That night, while he oiled the shop's shutters, she sat on the step. 'Abbu, can I explain my plan before you decide?' He grunted. 'Aditi is coming too. We'll take the four-thirty bus back, skip the last session. I'll call you when we leave and when we reach the chowk.' He kept oiling. 'And if the bus is late?' 'Then I call, and you or Chacha come. I've saved the number of the conductor too.' He was quiet a long time. 'Try it for the first week.' She kept every call.

qa.q: Which bus did Zainab promise to take back?
qa.a: The four-thirty bus back, skipping the last session.

qa.q: What was Abbu worried about?
qa.a: He was nervous about Zainab travelling back after dark.

qa.q: What made Zainab's request easier for Abbu to accept?
qa.a: She asked calmly, came with a detailed plan with a friend and check-in calls, and accepted a trial week.

qa.q: How might keeping every call change Abbu's trust in future?
qa.a: It shows him she's responsible, so he may allow her more freedom next time.

grounding: Shows a teen negotiating independence and trust with a parent respectfully in a small town.

passage: In their narrow Osaka apartment, Hiroshi, sixteen, set down two cups of tea before asking. His mother raised an eyebrow. 'That's suspicious.' 'The concert's on Saturday. It ends at ten-thirty.' 'The last train home is almost midnight. No.' He had expected that. 'Astrid's mother is picking both of us up from the venue. I'll share my location the whole time. And if I miss anything, you can say no to the next one.' His father looked up from his newspaper. 'Ten-thirty ends. Home by eleven-fifteen?' 'Eleven-fifteen.' His mother sighed and sipped her tea. 'Text me when it ends.' At ten thirty-two, her phone buzzed: 'Done. With Astrid's mum.' At eleven-ten he was in the doorway.

qa.q: Who was picking Hiroshi up from the concert?
qa.a: Astrid's mother was picking him and Astrid up from the venue.

qa.q: Why did Hiroshi make tea before asking?
qa.a: He wanted to soften the moment and show respect, expecting his parents to be cautious about his request.

qa.q: What made Hiroshi's negotiation work?
qa.a: He expected the concern, offered a safe ride and location sharing, and agreed to earn the next outing by keeping this one.

qa.q: How might his mother feel when he walked in at eleven-ten?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and more ready to trust him with the next request. 😊

grounding: Shows a teen negotiating a curfew and building trust with parents outside India.

passage: Harsha's mock test rank came on the coaching centre board in Hyderabad: 312. Last month it had been 48. She stood on the stairs, stomach empty, while other students pushed past. At home, Nanna said, 'Your cousin Sanjay stayed in the top fifty,' and went back to his phone. Harsha went to her room and stared at the ceiling. 'Maybe I'm just stupid.' Her sister Gargi came in with two cups of tea. 'One test. Which section dropped?' 'Chemistry.' 'Only chemistry?' Harsha checked. It was. Gargi said, 'So you're not stupid. You have a chemistry problem.' Harsha laughed a little. Later, she knocked on Nanna's door. 'Nanna, when you compare me to Sanjay, it makes me want to give up. Can you just ask me what went wrong?'

qa.q: What was Harsha's rank this month, and what had it been last month?
qa.a: It was 312 this month, and it had been 48 last month.

qa.q: What does Harsha saying 'Maybe I'm just stupid' reveal about her feelings?
qa.a: She was letting one bad rank make her doubt her whole worth, feeling hopeless after the comparison.

qa.q: How did Gargi help without dismissing Harsha's worry?
qa.a: She asked which section dropped, which turned a crushing rank into one specific problem Harsha could work on.

qa.q: How might Nanna feel when Harsha asks him not to compare her?
qa.a: He might feel surprised or a little defensive at first, but it gives him a chance to support her better.

grounding: Shows a teen coping with a rank drop and parental comparison without losing her self-worth.

passage: 'Papa, results are out.' Anand looked up from the laptop. 'And?' 'Seventy-eight percent.' 'Hmm. Mehta's daughter got ninety-two.' Disha's face went still. 'Can you not? Just once?' 'I'm only saying, beta, you're capable of more.' 'I know I'm capable! I studied every day for three months. I got stuck on maths. I'm still proud of English.' Anand closed the laptop. 'I didn't know about maths.' 'Because you only asked about marks.' Silence. 'What was hard?' 'Probability. I panicked.' 'We'll find a tutor for that, if you want. And English? Show me.' She handed over the marksheet. 'Ninety-one.' He smiled for the first time. 'Better than Mehta's daughter.' 'Papa!' 'Sorry, sorry. Better than last year.'

qa.q: What percentage did Disha get overall?
qa.a: She got seventy-eight percent.

qa.q: How did Disha feel when Papa mentioned Mehta's daughter?
qa.a: She was hurt and frustrated, her face going still, because she had worked hard and felt compared again.

qa.q: What turned the conversation around?
qa.a: Papa closed the laptop and asked what was hard, so they could focus on her effort and a real plan for maths.

qa.q: What might Papa realise from Disha's 'Because you only asked about marks'?
qa.a: He might realise his focus on marks and comparisons made her hide her struggles from him.

grounding: Shows a teen coping with marks and parental comparison and keeping her self-worth through honest talk.
